title: Assumable Mortgages: A Practical Guide for Real Estate Agents
description: Assumable mortgages explained for agents: which FHA and VA loans qualify, how the equity gap works, and what sellers need to know before accepting an offer.
keywords: assumable mortgage for real estate agents
image_alt: A hand holding out a set of house keys at an open front door

faq.q: Can a conventional loan be assumed?
faq.a: Usually not. Most conventional loans have a due-on-sale clause that requires the loan to be paid off when the home sells. FHA and VA loans are the most common assumable loans.

faq.q: Does a buyer have to be a veteran to assume a VA loan?
faq.a: No. A non-veteran can assume a VA loan if they qualify with the servicer, but the seller's VA entitlement generally stays tied to the loan unless an eligible veteran buyer substitutes their own entitlement.

faq.q: What is the equity gap in an assumption?
faq.a: It's the difference between the purchase price and the remaining loan balance. The buyer must cover it with cash, allowable gift funds, or a second mortgage where permitted.
The seller's current loan servicer reviews the buyer's credit, income, and assets under the loan program's rules and approves or denies the assumption.

body_html:
Here's a listing conversation I hear more and more: the seller bought or refinanced a few years ago, their mortgage carries a rate far below what buyers are seeing today, and someone asks, "Can the buyer just take over my loan?" Sometimes the answer is yes. That's an assumable mortgage, and for agents in Southern California it can be a real point of difference on the right listing. It can also blow up an escrow if nobody understands how it works.

This guide covers what agents need to know: which loans can be assumed, how the process runs, where the cash gap comes from, and how to set expectations with sellers and buyers before anyone signs.

What an assumable mortgage actually is

An assumption means the buyer takes over the seller's existing loan: the same remaining balance, the same interest rate, and the same remaining term. The buyer doesn't get a new loan at today's pricing. They step into the seller's shoes, with the servicer's approval.

Why this matters right now: a large share of homeowners are still holding mortgages with rates well below current averages. You can see the spread for yourself by comparing Freddie Mac's weekly Primary Mortgage Market Survey with the outstanding-loan data in FHFA's National Mortgage Database dashboard. When a seller's rate is meaningfully lower than the market, an assumable loan becomes a feature worth putting in front of buyers.

Which loans can be assumed (and which usually can't)

Not every mortgage is assumable, and the loan type is the first thing to confirm. In general:

  • FHA loans are generally assumable. For loans originated in the last few decades, the buyer must go through a creditworthiness review, and FHA's rules are set out in HUD's Single Family Housing Policy Handbook 4000.1. Assumptions are typically limited to buyers who will live in the home.
  • VA loans are generally assumable, and the buyer does not have to be a veteran. The buyer still has to qualify, and there are entitlement issues for the seller (more on that below). VA's program basics are on VA.gov.
  • USDA loans can be assumable in some cases, subject to program approval.
  • Most conventional loans include a due-on-sale clause, which means the loan must be paid off when the home sells. With rare exceptions, a typical conventional fixed-rate loan is not assumable.

Before you market a listing as assumable, have the seller pull their note or call their servicer and confirm in writing. "I think it's FHA" is not enough.

How the assumption process works

An assumption runs through the seller's current loan servicer, not through a lender the buyer picks. That changes the rhythm of the deal. Here's the usual flow:

  1. Confirm eligibility. The seller verifies the loan type, current balance, and whether the servicer processes assumptions.
  2. Buyer applies with the servicer. The buyer submits income, asset, and credit documentation, much like a regular application.
  3. Servicer underwrites the buyer. For FHA and VA, the buyer has to meet credit and income standards.
  4. Cover the equity gap. The buyer brings cash or arranges secondary financing for the difference between the price and the loan balance.
  5. Release and close. The seller should seek a formal release of liability so they are no longer on the hook for the loan after closing.

Servicers vary widely in how fast and how smoothly they handle assumptions. Many treat them as a low-volume back-office task. Build your contract timelines with that in mind and confirm the servicer's expected process before you commit to dates. I cover how to structure timelines and protections in my guide to financing contingencies.

The equity gap: where most assumptions get stuck

This is the part that surprises people. The buyer only takes over the remaining loan balance. Everything above that, the seller's equity, has to be paid at closing.

In much of Southern California, where values have risen and sellers have been paying down principal, that gap can be large. A buyer who loves the idea of an assumption may not have the cash to cover it. Options to discuss with a loan officer include:

  • Cash from savings or other liquid assets.
  • Gift funds, where the program and servicer allow them.
  • A second mortgage behind the assumed loan, when the program rules and the second-lien lender allow it. The blended cost needs a careful look, because a second lien usually carries a higher rate than the assumed loan.

The takeaway for agents: qualify the buyer's cash position early. An assumable loan only helps the buyer who can actually bridge the gap.

What sellers need to understand

Sellers often hear "assumable" and think it's all upside. Walk them through these points:

  • Release of liability. Without a formal release from the servicer, the seller could remain responsible if the buyer defaults later. Make sure the release is part of the plan.
  • VA entitlement. If a non-veteran assumes a VA loan, the seller's VA entitlement generally stays tied to that loan until it's paid off. If the buyer is an eligible veteran, they may be able to substitute their own entitlement, which frees up the seller's. A seller who plans to use a VA loan again should understand this before accepting an offer. My post on VA loan myths covers more on how entitlement works.
  • Timeline. An assumption can take longer than a standard purchase loan. Sellers who need to close by a specific date should weigh that.
  • Buyer pool. The equity gap can narrow the field of buyers who can make an assumption work, so price and terms still matter.

How to market and negotiate an assumable listing

When it fits, an assumable loan can make a listing stand out. A few practical habits:

  • Verify before you advertise. Confirm the loan type, balance, and servicer process. Be careful about publishing the seller's rate or payment in marketing; stick to describing the loan as assumable and let a loan officer walk qualified buyers through the specifics.
  • Explain it in plain English. Many buyers have never heard of an assumption. A one-page explainer in the listing packet goes a long way.
  • Compare both paths. Encourage buyers to have a loan officer compare an assumption plus any second lien against a new purchase loan. Sometimes the new loan wins once fees, second-lien costs, and timing are on the table.
  • Write the offer to match. Spell out the assumption, the servicer approval, the release of liability, and what happens if the servicer doesn't approve the buyer.

A quick comparison helps frame the conversation:

AssumptionNew purchase loan
Rate and termSeller's existing rate and remaining termCurrent market pricing
Who processes itSeller's servicerBuyer's chosen lender
Cash neededPrice minus loan balance (or a second lien)Down payment and closing costs
TimelineOften longer, servicer-dependentMore predictable
Seller considerationsRelease of liability; VA entitlementLoan paid off at closing

The takeaway for agents

Assumable mortgages aren't a gimmick, and they aren't magic. On the right listing, with the right buyer, they can be a real advantage. On the wrong one, they turn into a slow escrow and a frustrated seller.

The agents who do well with assumptions ask three questions early: Is the loan really assumable? Can the buyer cover the equity gap? Does the seller understand release of liability and, for VA loans, entitlement? Get clear answers to those and you'll know quickly whether an assumption is worth pursuing. If you have a listing or a buyer where this might fit, bring in a loan officer early to compare both paths side by side. Consult a tax or legal professional for questions about your clients' specific situations.
